unit.title: Communicate and interact effectively in the workplace

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Why is good communication important in a salon or spa?
options: It helps give clients the service they want, safely
It means that staff never need to write anything down
It lets staff talk about clients freely
It makes appointments shorter

questions.stem: Which of these is written communication in a salon?
options: A smile at a client
A talk with a co-worker
A client record card
A nod of the head

questions.stem: A client has just walked into the salon. What should you do first?
options: Finish your phone chat with a friend
Smile, make eye contact and greet her
Ask her to wait without looking up
Tell her the prices of every service the salon offers

questions.stem: Which way of speaking to a client is the most professional?
options: Using nicknames like 'darling' with every client
Speaking very fast so the client is not kept waiting
Using slang so the client feels at home
Using a clear, friendly voice and polite words

questions.stem: During a consultation, why should a therapist ask open questions?
options: To finish the consultation as quickly as she can
To get only 'yes' or 'no' answers
To get the client to say more about her needs
To avoid having to write anything down

questions.stem: Which of these is an open question for a facial consultation?
options: How does your skin feel at the end of the day?
Do you have oily skin on your forehead and nose?
Have you ever had a facial at any salon before?
Is your skin sensitive?

questions.stem: A client says, 'I just want a tidy-up of my brows.' How can the therapist make sure she understands what the client wants?
options: Start shaping at once and ask her about it after
Agree, then shape them as she prefers
Ask a co-worker what 'tidy-up' means
Repeat it back and agree the shape first

questions.stem: A client is telling you about a skin reaction she had last year. What should you do?
options: Keep looking at the booking screen while she talks
Listen, nod and ask questions to learn more
Tell her about your own reaction instead
Change the subject to something happier

questions.stem: Why should a therapist sum up the treatment plan at the end of a consultation?
options: To make the consultation take much longer
To check that she and the client agree
To show off her knowledge of the products
So she does not need to fill in the record card

questions.stem: A client is very quiet and gives short answers. What is the best approach?
options: Stop asking questions and just start
Talk loudly so she will join in
Ask the same question again and again until she answers
Be patient and ask gentle open questions

questions.stem: During a treatment, when is it best to keep conversation to a minimum?
options: When the client has shown she wants to relax
When you want to tell her all about your weekend
When you want to sell her a product
When a co-worker comes to chat

questions.stem: A client asks a question about a medical condition that you cannot answer. What should you do?
options: Make up an answer so that you seem like an expert
Tell her that it does not matter at all
Say you don't know and suggest she asks her doctor
Tell her to look it up on social media later

questions.stem: When explaining aftercare to a client, which is best?
options: Use long, technical words so that she trusts you more
Speak quickly while she pays at the front desk
Tell her once and assume she will remember
Use plain words and give a written sheet

questions.stem: A client cannot have her treatment today because of a possible skin infection. How should you tell her?
options: Calmly and privately, and suggest she sees a doctor
Loudly, so that everyone in the salon understands why
Quickly, then walk away to avoid upset
By text message after she leaves

questions.stem: Why do your posture and facial expression matter when you greet a client?
options: They show how much the treatment costs
They have no effect if your words are polite
They show the client whether she is welcome
They decide how long the treatment will take

questions.stem: During a massage, how should a therapist check that the pressure is right?
options: Wait until the end and ask then
Ask the client quietly and watch her reactions
Press harder and harder until the client complains
Assume it is fine if she says nothing

questions.stem: Why does a therapist's appearance (clean uniform, tidy hair, short nails) matter?
options: It lets her charge higher prices
It means that she does not need to speak to clients much
It decides which clients she is given
It shows care and professional standards

questions.stem: A client looks uncomfortable and keeps pulling the towel up during a back massage. What should the therapist do?
options: Ask if she is comfortable, and adjust the towels
Ignore it and carry on with the massage as planned
Tell her firmly to relax and stop moving about
Finish the massage early without a word

questions.stem: Why should staff respect clients' different cultures, beliefs and backgrounds?
options: So the salon can charge some clients more
Because the law says some groups must be treated better than others
So every client feels welcome and is treated fairly
So staff can avoid clients they do not understand

questions.stem: A client is hard of hearing. Which is the best way to communicate during the consultation?
options: Shout each word very loudly into her ear
Face her, speak clearly and write notes if needed
Speak only to the friend who came with her instead of to her
Speak quickly with your face turned away

questions.stem: A client uses a wheelchair. Who should you speak to about her treatment?
options: The client herself
The person pushing the wheelchair
The salon manager only
Nobody; just start the work

questions.stem: A visitor from overseas at a hotel spa does not understand the words 'patch test'. What should you do?
options: Say the same words again, more loudly
Skip the patch test to save her time
Hand her a leaflet and leave her to read it
Explain it simply and show her the steps

questions.stem: A client asks for a female therapist for religious reasons. What is the respectful response?
options: Tell her that the salon does not take special requests
Laugh it off and give her whoever is free
Arrange a female therapist, or offer another time
Tell her she is being difficult

questions.stem: Your supervisor gives you several jobs at once, and you cannot do them all before your next client. What should you do?
options: Do the easiest job, forget the rest
Tell her and ask which job comes first
Do them all quickly without care
Ask a client to help you

questions.stem: A new therapist joins the team today. What is the best way to welcome her?
options: Show her around, introduce her and offer help
Leave her to work everything out alone
Give her all the worst jobs to test her
Talk about her with the others behind her back

questions.stem: A therapist hands over a client to a co-worker at the change of shift. What should she tell the co-worker?
options: Only the latest gossip about the client
Nothing; the co-worker can work it out
Only the time the client arrived
What was done, what is left and any concerns

questions.stem: A busy co-worker needs help, and you have a free half hour. What is the best thing to do?
options: Take a long break in the staff room
Wait until the manager tells you to go and help her
Offer to help, such as preparing her next room
Tell her she should have planned better

questions.stem: Why should staff use the appointment book or booking system correctly?
options: So staff can choose the clients they like
So everyone knows who is booked, when and for what
So that clients are never able to change their appointments
So the manager can avoid talking to staff

questions.stem: Which is the most professional way to talk to co-workers in front of clients?
options: Use your private jokes and nicknames for each other
Talk about other clients' treatments
Argue openly so the client can take sides
Be polite and keep personal matters private

questions.stem: A client complains that her nail polish chipped the next day. What should you do first?
options: Listen calmly without interrupting
Tell her she must have damaged it
Argue that the polish is good quality
Walk away and get the manager

questions.stem: After listening to a client's complaint, what is the best next step?
options: Blame the co-worker who did the work
Promise a full refund every time
Apologise and agree on what will be done
Tell the client to write a letter

questions.stem: Why should a complaint be recorded and passed to the supervisor?
options: So the client can be banned
So it is followed up and the service improves
So the staff member can be fired
Because clients always like to see lots of paperwork

questions.stem: You disagree with a co-worker about whose turn it is to clean the wax area. What is the best first step?
options: Talk to her calmly in private
Complain about her to the clients
Refuse to speak to her all week
Post about it on your social media

questions.stem: Which of these is an 'I' statement that helps solve a disagreement without blame?
options: 'You always leave the trolley empty.'
'You never help anybody else at all in this salon, ever.'
'Everyone knows you are lazy.'
'I feel stressed when the trolley is not restocked.'

questions.stem: When should you ask your supervisor to help with a disagreement with a co-worker?
options: Straight away, before talking to the person
Never, because you must always sort out problems on your own
When talking calmly together has not solved it
Only after the problem has gone on for months

questions.stem: At a staff meeting, which behaviour is most helpful?
options: Look at your phone while the others are talking
Listen, wait your turn and keep to the point
Talk over others to get your point across
Stay silent even when you have a good idea

questions.stem: Who leads a meeting and keeps it to the agenda?
options: The newest member
The timekeeper
The guest
The chairperson

questions.stem: A co-worker tells you that your client records are hard to read. What is the best response?
options: Thank her and work on writing more clearly
Tell her that her own records are worse
Ignore it, as she is not your supervisor
Stop writing records so it never happens

questions.stem: A new trainee asks you how her first eyebrow wax went. Which reply is the most useful feedback?
options: 'It was fine, I suppose. Don't worry about it.'
'That was terrible. You should start all over again.'
'Good, even shape. Next time hold the skin tighter.'
'Ask someone else, I'm busy.'

questions.stem: A client sends a message to the salon's phone asking to change her booking. What should you do?
options: Ignore it until she phones the salon herself
Reply politely and update the booking
Reply with a joke and a long row of emojis
Remember the change but tell no one else

questions.stem: Which is the most professional message to send a client?
options: 'Hey hun!!! U still comin in today or wat?? Lmk asap!!!'
'Facial 2. Don't be late. If late, lose slot.'
'MS REID!!! DO NOT BE LATE FOR YOUR FACIAL AGAIN TODAY!!!'
'Hello Ms Reid, a reminder: your facial is at 2 p.m.'

questions.stem: A client's friend phones and asks what treatment the client had yesterday. What should you say?
options: Say politely that you cannot share client details
Tell her everything, since they are good friends
Read out the client's record card to her
Give her the client's phone number instead

questions.stem: Why must a client record card be filled in clearly and accurately?
options: So that the client can take it home as a souvenir
So the salon can sell the details to others
So any therapist can safely see what was done
So it looks neat on the shelf

questions.stem: Where is the best place to talk with a co-worker about a client's skin problem?
options: At the reception desk
In private, away from other clients
On the staff group chat, with the client's name
Loudly across the salon floor

questions.stem: A change to the salon's opening hours must reach all staff. Which is the best way?
options: Tell one person and hope that it spreads to the rest
Whisper it to the staff that you like best
Post a dated notice and tell the team
Write it on the back of a till receipt

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name of the form a client signs to show that she agrees to a treatment after it has been explained?
What is the name for messages sent without words, such as facial expression, posture and gestures?
What type of question can be answered with just 'yes' or 'no'?
What word means keeping a client's information private and not sharing it without her permission?
What is the name for listening with full attention, nodding and checking that you have understood?

essays.stem: Describe how a therapist should carry out a client consultation for a facial, from greeting the client to agreeing the treatment plan.
essays.modelAnswer: The therapist greets the client by name with a smile, introduces herself and takes her to a quiet, private area. She explains that she will ask some questions so that the facial is safe and suits her. She uses open questions, such as 'How does your skin feel during the day?', to learn about the client's skin, her routine and what she hopes for, and closed questions to check facts, such as allergies, medicines, pregnancy or recent sun damage. She listens carefully, keeps friendly eye contact, and writes the answers on the record card. She looks at the skin and checks for any contraindications; if she finds one, she explains kindly and refers the client to her doctor. She explains the treatment she suggests, the products, the time it takes and the price in J$, in plain words, and answers any questions. She sums up the plan to check that they agree, and the client signs the consultation form before the treatment starts.
markingPoints: Greets the client and takes her to a private area
Uses open and closed questions to find her needs and check for contraindications
Listens actively and records the answers on the record card
Explains the plan, products, time and price in plain words
Sums up to check agreement and gets the client's signature

essays.stem: Explain the difference between open and closed questions, and give an example of when a therapist would use each.
essays.modelAnswer: An open question cannot be answered with just 'yes' or 'no'. It usually starts with words such as what, how, why or 'tell me', and it gets the client to talk and give details. A therapist uses open questions at the start of a consultation to find out what the client wants and how she feels about her skin or nails, for example 'What would you like to change about your skin?' or 'How do you care for your nails at home?'. A closed question can be answered with 'yes', 'no' or a single fact. It is quick and useful for checking facts and for safety, for example 'Are you allergic to any products?', 'Are you taking any medicine?' or 'Is this pressure comfortable?'. A good consultation uses both kinds: open questions to understand the client, and closed questions to confirm the details and check that it is safe to go ahead.
markingPoints: Open questions cannot be answered yes or no, and they bring out details
A correct example of an open question in a salon
Closed questions get yes, no or a fact, and are quick for checking
A correct example of a closed question, such as about allergies
Both kinds are used together in a consultation

essays.stem: Explain how body language and tone of voice affect communication with clients, and give examples of good and poor body language in a salon.
essays.modelAnswer: Clients notice how we say things as much as what we say. If our body language or tone does not match our words, the client will believe the body language. A warm, calm tone makes a client feel welcome and relaxed, while a sharp, bored or rushed tone can make her feel unwanted, even if the words are polite. Good body language includes smiling, making friendly eye contact, standing or sitting up straight, facing the client, nodding while she talks, and keeping an open posture with relaxed arms. It also includes respecting her personal space and using a gentle, confident touch during treatments. Poor body language includes folding the arms, frowning, sighing, looking at a phone or the clock, turning away while the client is speaking, and chewing gum. Watching the client's body language helps too: if she looks tense or pulls away, the therapist should stop and check that she is comfortable.
markingPoints: Body language and tone can say more than the words
A warm tone welcomes; a sharp or bored tone puts clients off
Examples of good body language: smiling, eye contact, open posture, nodding
Examples of poor body language: folded arms, phone, turning away, sighing
Reads the client's body language and checks that she is comfortable

essays.stem: A client complains that her leg wax was too painful and has left red marks. Describe how you should deal with this.
essays.modelAnswer: I would take the client somewhere private and stay calm and polite. I would listen to the whole complaint without interrupting, and show that I understand how she feels, for example, 'I'm sorry it was so uncomfortable for you.' I would ask questions to understand what happened and look at the skin. Some redness after waxing is normal and usually settles, but if the skin is broken, very sore or blistered, I would give first aid as the salon's policy says, such as a cool compress, and suggest she sees a doctor. I would explain the aftercare again in plain words, for example avoiding hot baths, sun and perfumed products for as long as the aftercare sheet says, and give her the written sheet. I would tell my supervisor, who may offer a follow-up or another solution under the salon's policy. I would write the complaint and what was done on the record card and in the complaints record, and follow up with a call the next day.
markingPoints: Takes the client somewhere private, stays calm and listens without interrupting
Shows understanding and apologises
Checks the skin, gives first aid if needed, and refers her to a doctor if it is serious
Explains the aftercare and involves the supervisor in any solution
Records the complaint and follows it up

essays.stem: Describe common barriers to communication in a busy salon or spa, and explain how to overcome them.
essays.modelAnswer: Noise is a common barrier: dryers, music and other conversations make it hard to hear, so the therapist can move to a quieter area, turn the music down, or face the client and speak clearly. Language can be a barrier with visitors or clients who speak little English, so she uses simple words, gestures, pictures and a written price list. Jargon, such as 'exfoliation' or 'contraindication', can confuse clients, so she explains these terms in plain words. A hearing or sight difficulty can be overcome by facing the client, speaking clearly, and using large print or written notes. Strong feelings, such as anger or nerves, block listening, so she stays calm and gives the client time. Distractions, such as phones or being rushed, are removed by giving the client full attention. Guessing what the client wants is also a barrier, so she asks questions and checks her understanding by summing up.
markingPoints: Names noise and how to reduce it
Names language or jargon and how to overcome it
Names a hearing or sight difficulty and how to help
Names strong feelings or distractions and how to handle them
Checks understanding by asking questions and summing up

essays.stem: Explain how a salon team can work well together, and what each member can do to support the others.
essays.modelAnswer: A salon team works well when everyone knows their role and shares the goal of giving every client a safe, high-quality service. The manager makes roles, rotas and procedures clear, and holds short briefings so that everyone knows the day's bookings and any changes. Each member supports the others by arriving on time, keeping to the appointment times, and leaving shared areas clean and stocked for the next person. They share information, such as a client's allergy or a product running low, through the record cards, the booking system or a handover note. They offer help when a co-worker is busy, for example by setting up a room or greeting her next client. They speak respectfully, avoid gossip, and deal with disagreements calmly and in private. They give and accept fair feedback and share new skills. When everyone does this, the work runs smoothly, stress is lower, and clients notice the difference.
markingPoints: Clear roles, procedures and a shared goal
Good timekeeping, and shared areas left ready for others
Shares information through records, briefings or handovers
Helps busy co-workers and treats everyone with respect
Deals with disagreements calmly and gives fair feedback

essays.stem: A co-worker often leaves the shared treatment room untidy, and you are getting upset about it. Describe how you would deal with this in a professional way.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would calm down, so that I do not speak in anger or complain to other staff or to clients. I would choose a quiet time and a private place to talk to her, never in front of clients. I would use 'I' statements to explain the problem without blaming her, for example, 'I feel rushed when the room is not ready for my next client.' I would give a clear example and then listen to her side, because she may have a reason, such as bookings back to back. Together we would agree a solution, such as each person resetting the room straight after a client, or a checklist on the door. I would thank her for listening. If the problem keeps happening after we have talked, I would ask our supervisor to help, giving facts rather than opinions. All through, I would stay polite and keep working well with her.
markingPoints: Calms down first and does not complain to others or in front of clients
Talks to the co-worker privately at a suitable time
Uses 'I' statements and a clear example, without blame
Listens to her side and agrees a solution together
Asks the supervisor for help if it continues, giving facts

essays.stem: Describe how to take part well in a staff meeting, before, during and after the meeting.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the meeting, I read the agenda, think about the items, and bring any information or ideas I need, such as stock figures or a client's suggestion. I arrive on time with a pen and notebook and switch my phone to silent. During the meeting, I listen to each speaker without interrupting, wait my turn, and keep my points short and on the topic. I speak clearly and politely, give reasons for my ideas, and respect other people's views even when I disagree. If I do not understand something, I ask. I write down any task I agree to do, with its deadline. If I am the minute-taker or the timekeeper, I do that role carefully. After the meeting, I read the minutes, check that they are correct, and finish my tasks on time. I tell the chairperson if there is a problem with a task, and I pass on information to a co-worker who missed the meeting if I am asked to.
markingPoints: Before: reads the agenda, prepares and arrives on time
During: listens, waits to speak and keeps to the point
During: speaks politely, gives reasons and respects other views
Notes agreed tasks and deadlines, or carries out a meeting role
After: checks the minutes and completes tasks on time

essays.stem: Explain why client confidentiality matters, and how staff keep client information private in speech, in writing and online.
essays.modelAnswer: Clients share private details with a therapist, such as their health, medicines, skin problems, pregnancy, address and phone number. They trust the salon to keep these private. If the details are shared, the client could be embarrassed or harmed, she may stop coming, the salon's good name suffers, and the law on data protection may be broken. In speech, staff do not talk about clients by name at reception, with other clients or outside work, and they discuss a client's treatment only in private with staff who need to know. In writing, record cards and consultation forms are kept in a locked cabinet, not left on the desk, and hold only what is needed. Online, client files are protected with passwords, screens are locked, staff do not post photos of or comments about clients on social media without written permission, and messages go only to the client's own number. Staff never give out a client's details over the phone without her permission.
markingPoints: Explains what is private and why the client's trust matters
Gives a result of breaking confidentiality: harm, loss of clients, or breaking the law
In speech: no talk about clients in public or outside work
In writing: records locked away, holding only what is needed
Online and by phone: passwords, no social media posts without permission, no details given out

essays.stem: Explain how to give and receive feedback at work in a way that helps people improve.
essays.modelAnswer: When I give feedback, I choose a good time and a private place, and I ask the person if it is a good moment. I start with something specific that went well, then explain one or two things to improve, using clear examples about the work, not the person. For example, 'Your massage strokes were smooth; next time check the pressure with the client sooner.' I keep a calm, friendly tone, give a reason, suggest how to improve, and let the person ask questions. I never give feedback in anger or in front of clients. When I receive feedback, I listen without interrupting or making excuses, and I thank the person. I ask questions if I am not sure what they mean, and I think about it honestly. I decide what I will do to improve, try it, and may ask for more feedback later to check my progress. Feedback given and taken in this way builds skills and trust.
markingPoints: Gives feedback privately, at a good time, in a calm tone
Starts with what went well, then specific points about the work, not the person
Suggests how to improve and allows questions
Receives feedback by listening, thanking and asking questions, without excuses
Acts on the feedback and checks progress

practical1.title: Client consultation and booking: a role play with record cards
practical1.brief: As a group, act out client consultations in the Centre's salon or spa reception and treatment area. The assessor gives each member a client card, for example: a bride who wants a facial before her wedding, a visitor at a hotel spa who speaks little English, a client who is hard of hearing, an older client who uses a walking frame, or a regular client who mentions a new allergy. Each member plays the therapist once and the client once. As the therapist: greet the client, take her to a private area, use open and closed questions to find her needs and check for contraindications, write the answers on a consultation and record card, explain the treatment, the time and the price in J$ in plain words, sum up, and ask the 'client' to sign. Then book her next appointment in the appointment book and write a short, professional confirmation message on a message card. The other members watch and fill in an observation sheet for each consultation. Photograph each stage below (cards, hands and backs only, unless members agree and the Centre allows faces) and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the cards, the appointment page and the observation sheets once for the whole group.
materials: Client cards from the assessor (one for each member)
Blank consultation and record cards (at least 2 for each member)
A treatment price list in J$
A page of the appointment book, and message cards
Pens, clipboards, two chairs and a small table
A phone or camera for photos
photos: The consultation area set up, with the blank cards and the price list
Each member as the therapist during the consultation (from behind, or showing the card)
Each completed and signed consultation and record card
The appointment book page with the bookings
The completed observation sheets laid out together
checklist: Greeted the client politely and took her to a private area
Used open and closed questions suited to the client's needs
Listened actively and checked for contraindications
Adapted the communication for the client on the card (language, hearing or mobility)
Wrote accurate details clearly on the card
Explained the treatment, time and price in plain words, and summed up
Booked the appointment correctly and wrote a professional message
Gave fair, useful feedback on an observation sheet
safety: Keep walkways and fire exits clear, and keep bags and cables out of the way
Use only made-up names, numbers and health details, never real client records
If a member plays a client with a walking frame, move slowly and keep the floor clear

practical2.title: Handling a client complaint, then a team meeting to agree improvements
practical2.brief: This task has two parts. Part A: the assessor gives each member a complaint card, for example a chipped manicure, a long wait past the appointment time, a wax that felt too hot, or a client who was overcharged. In pairs, one member plays the client and the other deals with the complaint: take the client somewhere private, listen without interrupting, show understanding and apologise, ask questions, agree what will be done under the salon's policy, and fill in a complaint record. Swap, so that each member deals with one complaint. Part B: hold a 20-minute team meeting about the complaints. Give each member a role (chairperson, minute-taker, timekeeper, or member) and use an agenda that the group writes first: (1) welcome, (2) the complaints received, (3) their causes, (4) improvements, (5) actions and dates. Every member speaks at least once. Then write the minutes, an action plan with names and dates, and a short notice to staff about one change. Photograph each stage below (hands, backs and papers only, unless members agree and the Centre allows faces) and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the complaint records, the agenda, the minutes, the action plan and the notice once for the whole group.
materials: Complaint cards from the assessor (one for each member)
Paper for the agenda, the minutes and the action plan
A sheet of card and markers for the staff notice
A table and chairs for the meeting, and a clock or timer
A phone or camera for photos
photos: Each complaint role play, from behind or showing the form
The meeting in progress, with the timekeeper's clock showing
The minutes and the action plan
The finished staff notice on the board
checklist: Stayed calm and listened without interrupting
Showed understanding, apologised and agreed a fair solution under the policy
Filled in the complaint record accurately
Carried out the meeting role well (chairperson, minute-taker, timekeeper or member)
Spoke clearly, kept to the point and respected other views
Helped agree clear actions with names and dates
Wrote in plain, polite language in the minutes, the plan or the notice
safety: Keep the role play calm: no shouting and no touching
Use only made-up names and details
Keep walkways and fire exits clear during the meeting
